text: You can create and manage AD objects by hand with Active Directory Users and Computers, opened by running dsa.msc, which shows your domain's OU structure and lets you right-click to create a new user or group inside the right OU. That's fine for a handful of accounts. In this lesson we'll also cover the two kinds of groups AD supports, the three group scopes, and the PowerShell cmdlets that do the same work faster for dozens of accounts at once.

A security group can be granted permissions — to a file share, a printer, an application — because it has a security identifier NTFS and Group Policy can act on. A distribution group exists purely for email distribution lists and cannot be granted permissions to anything. Try to grant file access to a distribution group and it fails silently: the group shows up in the permission list, but nobody in it actually gets access.

Every group also has a scope. Domain local groups can hold members from anywhere in the forest but only grant permissions within their own domain, so they're typically the group actually applied to a resource. Global groups can only hold members from their own domain, but can grant permissions anywhere in the forest, so they typically represent a real-world group of people. The standard pattern, A-G-DL-P, nests a global group of people inside a domain local group that holds the permission.

PowerShell does the same work ADUC does with clicks. New-ADUser with a name, a SamAccountName, and a Path creates a user inside a specific OU in one line. Add-ADGroupMember then adds that user to a group, like Finance-Employees — the same A-G-DL-P pattern, done in two lines, and just as easy to repeat in a loop for twenty new hires instead of twenty trips through a wizard.

That covers the objects an OU structure actually holds — users, security groups, and the scope that governs how they're used. Next, we'll look at what those group memberships actually unlock on a file server: NTFS permissions, share permissions, and what happens when the two don't agree.
